newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.E. Asia currency war truce for bankers meeting.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asia currency war truce for bankers meeting.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies were on a firmer footing on Friday as the market paused from its recent frantic selling just in case an Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai sprang a surprise.
The meeting was expected to yield little more than warnings against currency speculation and talk of cooperation, but dealers said the market was taking nothing for granted.
"The market is cautious in case anything happens. I would advise customers to trim down their positions or just square up," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
Dealers said there were still some fears of concerted intervention to counter the recent series of attacks on regional currencies, but most were unconvinced.
"In general, it looks like the central banks have decided not to waste foreign exchange reserves intervening against market forces," a senior dealer at another European bank said.
Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Joseph Yam told reporters in Shanghai he was not worried about speculators attacking the Hong Kong dollar, pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.
Fears of a speculative attack on Asia's most strongly defended peg were triggered on Thursday when forward rates shot up in Hong Kong.

But the market was calmer on Friday and the Hong Kong dollar traded in a range after the HKMA released figures showing it held HK$569 billion at end June, up 6.4 percent from end December, a move seen as aimed at scaring off speculators.

In Thailand, the baht recovered some ground after the central Bank of Thailand deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said the currency's fall to 32 to the U.S. dollar was too far and that he did not expect the baht to fall much further.
It was at 31.950/32.020 to the dollar at 0845 GMT onshore against 31.950/32.350 earlier. It was at 31.750/31.900 offshore.
Some Bangkok dealers said they saw strong support for the baht around the 32.30 level in the morning, but they were not sure whether the central bank had intervened in the market.
The Singapore dollar firmed through the 1.47 to the U.S. dollar level as London-based parties sold dollars. It was at 1.4675/85 to the U.S. dollar at 0845 GMT.

Its recovery from a low of 1.4765 had spurred talk of possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, but most dealers attributed the move to nervous profit-taking after the U.S. dollar's spike up in last two days.
Selling of the Malaysian ringgit subsided but the market remained volatile and subject to sharp moves amid thin volumes and wide spreads.
Dealers said the ringgit's recovery was blocked around 2.64 to the dollar and more weakness was likely in the near term.

"I don't think dollar/ringgit has seen a top yet. It should go to 2.70 eventually and the recent low of 2.6180/2.6200 should hold," a Singapore-based dealer said. The ringgit was at 2.6475/95 to the dollar at 0845 GMT.
The Indonesian rupiah remained depressed below the 2,600 level to the dollar, but dealers said activity had slowed. Spot rupiah was at 2,605/15 at 0845 GMT after opening at 2,601/09.
The Philippine peso ended weaker in very light trade as banks sold dollars to commercial clients rather than the interbank market, where the central bank was seen capping the selling rate.
The central bank sold dollars from 28.49 to 28.45 early in the day, but this was done on a selective basis, turning off many potential sellers. The peso ended at 28.50 against 28.47 on Thursday.
